A tourist who recently returned from a visit to the Kisumu develops the signs and symptoms of malaria (fever, chills, muscle aches & fatigue). Blood tests reveal the presence of chloroquine-sensitive P. falciparum. Chloroquine therapy is initiated, resulting in a gradual disappearance of malarial symptoms. What is the primary antimalarial mechanism of action of this drug?

Shortly after returning from a medical mission in Kilifi, a 25-year-old medical student develops flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, headache, and sweating. Blood samples are positive for the presence of chloroquine-resistant P. vivax. Prior to initiating combination drug therapy, the WHO recommends that a blood test for G6PD be performed in order to avoid producing a potentially fatal drug-induced hemolytic anemia. Which of the following drugs, if used in treatment, would MOST LIKELY cause this serious side effect?

The patient suffering from infection with P. vivax recovers from malarial symptoms, but then suffers a relapse several months later after discontinuation of drug therapy. A decision is made to initiate therapy to specifically target the hepatic stage of the parasite. Which of following medications would be the most appropriate choice?

A patient on multi-drug therapy for P. falciparum malaria seeks medical attention in the Emergency Department of University Hospital for an episode of vertigo, dizziness, nausea & vomiting. Examination of the patient's ECG reveals a markedly prolonged QTc interval. Which of the following drugs in the patient's drug regimen is most likely responsible for these side effects?

An HIV-positive patient is being initialized on combination antiretroviral therapy (cART). One of the drugs included is a drug that has no direct antiviral effect, but inhibits CYP3A4. Inclusion of this drug prolongs the duration of action of other CYP3A substrates (such as protease inhibitors), which reduces the daily pill burden. Which drug serves this purpose?

You are caring for a patient recently diagnosed with HIV infection, and plan to initiate therapy with an effective cART regimen. Two components of the drug regimen to be implemented include a combination of a protease inhibitor and pharmacokinetic booster (lopinavir + ritonavir) and a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (zidovudine). What other additional drugmay also be included to provide the most effective treatment?

When designing an effective cART regimen for treating a patient's HIV infection, there are certain drug combinations that should be avoided due to either a higher incidence of toxic side effects, or antagonism of each other's effects on HIV replication. If a patient's drug regimen included the NRTI zidovudine, what other drug should be avoided?
Patients on cART can experience drug toxicities that are common for most drugs within the same class. Which toxicity would be expected for a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor?
Most formulations of cART contain a protease inhibitor (PI). Which of the following side effects is commonly observed in patients following initiation of therapy with this class of drug?

NRTIs are considered the backbone of cART. This class of drugs can cause a variety of side effects & toxicity including neuropathy, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, hepatic steatosis & lactic acidosis. What molecular mechanism is the most likely cause for these adverse effects?

Not all inhibitors of viral reverse transcriptase require intracellular phosphorylation to an active triphosphate form. Which of the following is an example of a RT inhibitor that does not require intracellular activation, and binds to a different site compared to those that do?

Entry inhibitors are frequently added as a component of cART for treatment-experienced patients who have persistent HIV-1 replication, despite ongoing therapy. One such agent binds selectively to the CCR5 host protein, one of two cytokine receptors necessary for the entrance of HIV into CD4+ cells. Its use is limited to patients that have a strain of HIV that utilizes CCR5 exclusively for cell entry, and do not utilize CXCR4 or other chemokine receptors. Which agent is this?
Several drugs used to treat the flu work by blocking the viral endonuclease. Which drug works by this mechanism?

Michael is an 8-year-old boy who is brought to the emergency department by his mother after he returns home from school complaining of flu-like symptoms. Because he has difficulty swallowing tablets (like many children under the age of 10), you decide to prescribe a flu medication that can be inhaled, instead of swallowed. What is the active ingredient for the medication you will prescribe?

An HIV immune compromised patient develops a severe case of CMV retinitis that requires treatment. Before prescribing the drug of choice, you explain to your patient that it needs to be taken orally twice daily, and that a follow-up visit for blood tests is needed to monitor for possible decreased levels of red cells, white cells, and platelets. The drug having this pharmacologic profile is:

An "anti-influenza" medication no longer recommended by the CDC as a treatment for the flu due to the development of high levels of drug resistance.

A 42 year hospitalized patient with an indwelling central venous catheter develops a life-threating infection by a drug-resistant form of Candida albicans. A decision is made to treat the patient with a liposomal infusion containing an antifungal drug that acts by binding to ergosterol, creating large pores in the fungal cell membrane that cause leakage of cellular components, resulting in cell death. Which antifungal drug was used to treat this patient's resistant infection?

A debilitated cancer patient who has undergone several rounds of chemotherapy is given a series of antibiotics to treat a presumed bacterial infection. When symptoms of infection persist, a fresh blood sample is taken for analysis, and comes back positive for Candida albicans. The patient is given an i.v. infusion of an antifungal drugs, and shortly thereafter develops chills, fever, vomiting and hypotension. What antifungal drug was most likely given?

JH is a 21-year-old-woman who comes to your Ob/Gyn clinic with a chief complaint of vaginal soreness and a burning discomfort during urination. A pelvic exam reveals signs of inflammation and discharge. A quick microscopic exam of the discharge indicates the presence of a yeast infection. You review the list of JH's current medications, which include an estrogen/progesterone oral contraceptive, and a daily multivitamin. You the administer an oral dose of 150 mg fluconazole to treat her infection. For what reason did you review her current list of medications?
options: Fluconazole's bioavailability is low, and may be affected by other drugs
Fluconazole can induce cyp P-450 and increase the hepatic clearance of other drugs
Fluconazole is a CYP P-450 inhibitor, and can decrease the metabolism of other drugs
Fluconazole enhances the renal clearance of several drugs by inhibiting p-glycoprotein.

A.stem: A patient suffering from severe cryptococcal pneumonia is given combination therapy with flucytosine and amphotericin B. Other than the integrity of the fungal cell membrane, what other molecular target is affected by this drug combination?

A 65-year-old patient presents with a chief complaint of discolored toenails that have recently begun to cause mild pain and discomfort. Histological analysis of an under-nail swab is positive for Trichophyton rubrum. What oral medication would be the best choice to treat this infection?

A 57-year-old woman who has been on chronic therapy with corticosteroids for arteritis presents with a high fever, severe headache and neck stiffness. She also admits to feeling confused and irritable, and having felt nauseous over the past 24 hours. A lumbar puncture is used to obtain a sample of CSF, which reveals the presence of Cryptococcus neoformans in culture. The patient is admitted to hospital and you start an induction antifungal protocol with i.v. amphotericin B plus flucytosine for 2 weeks. Her condition slowly improves and you decide to switch her to an oral maintenance therapy which she will likely need to continue for up to a year after discharge from the hospital. Which agent would be the best choice for maintenance therapy?
An immunocompromised patient suffering from HIV is diagnosed with subacute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. Which drug would be the best choice for monotherapy?

An elderly man with a 20 yr history of atrial fibrillation arrives to your clinic complaining of weakness and recent episodes of bloody stool. When taking his medical history, he mentions having to watch his dietary intake of leafy vegetables (such as spinach), and having recently seen a dermatologist who placed him on fluconazole therapy for a skin infection (mucocutaneous candidiasis). What is the most likely explanation for this patient's most recent symptoms?
options: Worsening of the infection by Candida spp

Based upon the appearance of his sores, a tentative diagnosis of genital herpes is made. Lab tests indicate the presence of elevated liver enzymes, and both Hep C antibody & viral RNA. A diagnosis of active HCV infection is made. Which drug combination would be the best choice for treatment?
